questions.question: What are the seven fields in a scope contract?
options: title, description, owner, priority, deadline, status, tags
task_id, goal, allowed_files, forbidden_files, acceptance_criteria, rollback_plan, approvals_required
scope, budget, timeline, deliverables, risks, dependencies, success_metrics
input, output, constraints, assumptions, preconditions, postconditions, invariants
questions.explanation: A scope contract has: task_id (links to board), goal (one verifiable sentence), allowed_files (globs the agent may write), forbidden_files (globs must not touch even by accident), acceptance_criteria (test commands proving done), rollback_plan (operator runbook), and approvals_required (actions needing human sign-off).

questions.question: Why are globs preferred over raw file paths in scope contracts?
options: Globs are faster to evaluate
Real repos move files; globs (app/**/*.py) survive a refactor between sessions that would invalidate a raw path contract
Globs use less storage space
Globs are supported by all version control systems
questions.explanation: Raw paths become stale when files are renamed or moved during refactoring. Globs like app/**/*.py or tests/test_signup*.py continue matching the right files even after a refactor between sessions.

questions.question: The 'specsmaxxing' practice of writing scope contracts before invoking the agent reduced what metric from 52% to 21%?
options: Task failure rate
Rabbit-hole rate (scope creep incidents)
Token usage per task
Time to complete tasks
questions.explanation: A practitioner using 'specsmaxxing' (scope contracts in YAML before invoking the agent) reported the rabbit-hole rate (scope creep incidents) dropped from 52% to 21% in three weeks. The contract did the work, not the model.

questions.question: What is the 'violation budget' pattern in scope checking?
options: Allowing a certain number of failed tasks before raising an alert
Minor scope slips within a budget trigger warnings; only when the budget is exceeded does the merge gate refuse — allows a gate that ships vs one that gets disabled
Tracking the cost of scope violations over time
Setting a maximum number of files the agent is allowed to touch
questions.explanation: agent-guardrails ships a violationBudget per task: minor scope slips within budget surface as warnings; only when exceeded does the merge gate refuse. This is the difference between a gate teams respect vs one they disable because it's too strict.

questions.question: What does the rollback plan field in a scope contract enforce about thinking?
options: It enforces that all changes are reversible
Listing a rollback plan forces the contract author to think about what could go wrong — a contract without a rollback plan should not be approved
It provides a template for automated rollback scripts
It determines the maximum risk level for the task
questions.explanation: Including a rollback plan forces the author to reason about failure modes. 'A contract you cannot roll back from is a contract that should not be approved.' This is a quality gate for the task definition, not just for the agent's execution.

questions.question: What is the multi-contract merge semantics for allowed_files?
options: Union both allowed_files lists (the path allowed by either contract is allowed)
Intersect both allowed_files lists (both contracts must permit the path)
Use the more permissive contract's allowed_files
Use the most recently created contract's allowed_files
questions.explanation: When two scope contracts apply, merge semantics follow least privilege: allowed_files is intersected (both must permit), forbidden_files is unioned (either can prohibit), time_budget_minutes uses the minimum, approvals_required accumulates.
